H1.text: Sit in a train, and the train beside you seems to stand still. Stand on the platform, and it rushes past.

H2.text: So which is true? Is that train moving or not?

H3.text: Aarav sees the same puzzle on his bicycle ride to college.

H4.text: A friend cycling beside him at the same speed looks frozen. A bus coming the other way seems to fly past.

H5.text: Both views are true. By the end of this video, you will solve it with one subtraction.

P2.text: It is the velocity of one object, as seen by another object that may itself be moving.

P3.text: The velocity of B, as seen from A, is written v B A.

P4.text: The rule. v B A equals v B minus v A. The other one's velocity, minus the watcher's.

S1.text: Let's test it on our motion notebook.

S2.text: Bus A moves at six metres per second. Bus B, ahead of it, moves at four, the same way.

S3.text: From the ground, both move forward. A slowly catches up.

S4.text: Now ride inside bus A. Switch the view.

S5.text: From A, bus A is still. And bus B drifts backward, toward A.

S6.text: Four minus six is minus two metres per second. Minus means backward.

S7.text: Now bus B turns around, and comes toward A at four metres per second.

S8.text: Slow motion replay. From A, B rushes in at minus four minus six. Minus ten metres per second.

S9.text: Same speeds. Only the direction changed, and the relative speed jumped from two to ten.

D1.text: Where does the rule come from? One step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. The position of B as seen from A is the gap between them. x B A equals x B minus x A.

D3.text: Step two. Divide each change by the same small time, to see how fast the gap changes.

D4.text: Step three. Change in x B over time is v B. Change in x A over time is v A. So v B A equals v B minus v A.

D5.text: Step four. Swap the watcher, and only the sign flips. v A B equals minus v B A.

T1.text: Remember this. Relative velocity is the other one's velocity minus your own.

R1.text: A position time graph explains the frozen bus.

R2.text: Each bus gets a line. The vertical gap between the lines is x B A.

R3.text: Parallel lines have the same slope. So the buses have the same velocity.

R4.text: Then the gap never changes. And a gap that never changes means v B A is zero.

R5.text: That is why a friend cycling beside Aarav looks frozen. To him, the friend is at rest.

K1.text: Side by side. Two cars, at twenty and fifteen metres per second, going the same way.

K2.text: Relative velocity is twenty minus fifteen, five metres per second.

K3.text: Now the cars go opposite ways. Fifteen becomes minus fifteen. Twenty minus minus fifteen is thirty five.

K4.text: Your turn. Two cyclists ride toward each other, each at five metres per second. How fast does the gap close? Pause and decide.

K5.text: Ten metres per second! Opposite directions, so five minus minus five gives ten.

B1.text: One more. Two lines on a position time graph cross. What happens at that moment? Pause and think.

B2.text: They meet! Where the lines cross, both are at the same place at the same time.

W2.text: A car at seventy two kilometres per hour is a hundred and fifty metres behind a bus at fifty four. When does it catch up?

W3.text: Change to metres per second. Seventy two becomes twenty. Fifty four becomes fifteen.

W4.text: Relative velocity of the car, seen from the bus, is twenty minus fifteen. Five metres per second.

W5.text: From the bus, the car must close a gap of one hundred and fifty metres at five metres per second.

W6.text: One fifty divided by five is thirty. The car catches up in thirty seconds.

X2.text: Two trains move opposite ways at twenty and fifteen. Many students write twenty minus fifteen, five.

X3.text: But direction goes in as a sign. So it is twenty minus minus fifteen. Thirty five.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As short numericals: crossing trains, overtaking cars and meeting times.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A one hundred and fifty metre train runs east at fifty four kilometres per hour. A one hundred metre train runs west at thirty six. How long do they take to cross completely? Pause and solve.

Z1.text: The answer is B. Ten seconds.

Z2.text: Fifty four is fifteen metres per second. Thirty six is ten. Opposite ways, so the relative speed is twenty five.

Z3.text: To cross completely, they must close both lengths, two hundred and fifty metres. Divided by twenty five, that is ten seconds.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why does a bus moving beside you at the same speed look still?

Y3.text: Two. Why do speeds add when two objects move toward each other?

Y4.text: Three. If v B A is five metres per second, what is v A B?

N1.text: Next time: five newtons plus five newtons can give ten newtons, or zero. How? Find out in scalars and vectors, the first topic of chapter three.
